text: Polaris is Microsoft's cloud-native distributed SQL query engine, originally built for Azure Synapse, with two design goals: converge data-warehouse and big-data workloads on one engine, and fully separate compute from state so execution is stateless and elastically scalable.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: Polaris abstracts every dataset as a grid of data cells indexed on two dimensions: a user-defined partition function used for aggressive partition pruning under range or equality predicates, and a system-chosen hash-distribution function that maps rows to many buckets so cells (and therefore computation) can be spread across arbitrarily many compute nodes.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: The cell abstraction makes the distributed query processor storage-agnostic: the DQP operates only at cell granularity while single-node extraction of data inside a cell is delegated to the local execution engine, letting the same scale-out framework query analytical stores (ADLS, Parquet, Delta) and transactional stores alike.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: Polaris compute is stateless because all durable state — data, metadata, and transaction logs — is externalized to remote storage and centralized highly-available services; only caches live on compute nodes, and since caches can be rebuilt lazily from persisted data their loss never fails in-flight work, enabling partial query restarts and online topology changes.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: Polaris injects 'data move enforcer' operators — hash re-distribution and broadcast — to change a dataset's distribution properties; enforcers are blocking, must persist all output cells before consumers start, and the operator subtree rooted at an enforcer defines the input/output boundary of a task.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: A Polaris task is the physical execution of an operator expression over one hash-distribution of its inputs and has three components: input cell collections, a task template (the code for the expression), and an output cell collection; a query plan therefore becomes a DAG of task templates whose edges encode dataflow and precedence constraints.

sources.title: POLARIS: The Distributed SQL Engine in Azure Synapse (PVLDB 13(12), 2020)

text: Polaris deliberately makes tasks maximal units of work (e.g., fusing multiple hash-aligned joins into one task) and re-encodes each task template back into T-SQL that runs natively in a SQL Server instance on the compute node, so the engine combines big-data style scale-out with SQL Server's mature scale-up columnar execution, and the blocking task boundaries let SQL Server re-optimize with fresh statistics on intermediate results.

text: Throttling is staged progressively across four thresholds keyed to how much future capacity has been consumed: up to 10 minutes of future usage triggers no throttling (overage protection); between 10 and 60 minutes triggers a 20-second delay on new interactive operations; between 60 minutes and 24 hours causes interactive operations to be rejected outright while background operations may still start; beyond 24 hours all new requests — interactive and background alike — are rejected.

sources.title: Understand your Fabric capacity throttling

text: When accumulated future-capacity usage exceeds the 10-minute overage protection window, the excess is recorded as carryforward CUs. Each subsequent timepoint that has idle capacity reduces this carryforward balance through a process called burndown. Throttling enforcement continues until the full carryforward balance reaches zero.

sources.title: Understand your Fabric capacity throttling

text: Operations that were already in flight when a capacity enters a throttling state are always allowed to run to completion; only new operation submissions are subject to delay or rejection.

sources.title: Understand your Fabric capacity throttling

text: Fabric's native execution engine (NEE) is built on two open-source components: Velox, a C++ database acceleration library from Meta that performs vectorized execution, and Apache Gluten (incubating), a middle layer from Intel that offloads execution from JVM-based SQL engines to native engines.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: Gluten intercepts the optimized Spark SQL physical plan and converts supported portions into a Substrait plan, which Velox then executes as vectorized, SIMD-accelerated, columnar C++ code in place of the JVM operator implementations.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: The accelerated execution path runs transparently under existing SQL: queries do not need to be rewritten or specially hinted to benefit from GPU execution, since the engine decides internally which query fragments are eligible for acceleration.

sources.title: CoddSpeed: Hardware Accelerated Query Processing in Microsoft Fabric (SIGMOD 2026 Industrial Track, Best Paper)

text: CoddSpeed's execution engine descends from the Tensor Query Processor (TQP) research lineage, which reformulates relational operators such as filter/select, join, group-by, and order-by as operations executable on a tensor computation runtime rather than as traditional row- or column-oriented CPU operators.

sources.title: CoddSpeed: Hardware Accelerated Query Processing in Microsoft Fabric (SIGMOD 2026 Industrial Track, Best Paper)

text: The tensor-computation approach targets PyTorch as its execution runtime, treating it as a hardware-abstraction layer: because PyTorch already supports diverse accelerators, expressing relational operators as tensor operations lets the same operator implementations run without hardware-specific rewrites.

sources.title: CoddSpeed: Hardware Accelerated Query Processing in Microsoft Fabric (SIGMOD 2026 Industrial Track, Best Paper)

text: The production architecture is organized around two abstraction layers: a coprocessor abstraction layer that routes eligible query fragments to accelerator hardware, and a data abstraction layer that unifies caching and data movement across CPU and GPU memory so accelerated and non-accelerated operators can be mixed within one query plan.

sources.title: CoddSpeed: Hardware Accelerated Query Processing in Microsoft Fabric (SIGMOD 2026 Industrial Track, Best Paper)

text: The system is explicitly designed for 'hardware independence': the abstraction layering exists so the warehouse can target GPUs today and extend to other accelerator classes such as FPGAs or ASICs later, without redesigning the query engine or its SQL-facing behavior.

sources.title: CoddSpeed: Hardware Accelerated Query Processing in Microsoft Fabric (SIGMOD 2026 Industrial Track, Best Paper)

text: The paper reports the accelerated path outperforming the equivalent CPU-only execution by more than an order of magnitude across a mix of production and benchmark scenarios, framing this as a general characteristic of eligible workloads rather than an isolated best case.

text: Data Factory is Fabric's data integration workload: it connects to data sources, moves data, transforms it, and orchestrates movement and transformation tasks from a single place, with connectivity to more than 170 data sources spanning cloud, multicloud, and on-premises systems reached through gateways.

sources.title: What is Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

text: Microsoft positions Data Factory in Fabric as the next generation of Azure Data Factory, and publishes a comparison guide plus a migration guide for moving Azure Data Factory and Azure Synapse pipelines into Fabric.

sources.title: What is Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

text: Data Factory offers three distinct data-movement options: Copy job for simplified movement with built-in delivery styles (bulk, incremental, and change-data-capture replication), Copy activity for fully customizable movement with manual control of parallelism, and Mirroring for near-real-time database replication into OneLake.

sources.title: What is Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

text: The Copy activity runs on a serverless architecture that exposes parallelism at three distinct levels: control flow can launch many copy activities concurrently (for example inside a ForEach loop), each activity can scale its own compute via intelligent throughput optimization, and within one activity multiple threads read from the source and write to the destination in parallel.

sources.title: Copy activity performance and scalability guide (Fabric Data Factory)

text: Intelligent throughput optimization (ITO) is the Copy activity's compute-sizing lever: the service weighs CPU, memory, network allocation, and the expected cost of the run to pick a throughput level. It accepts the presets Auto, Standard, Balanced, and Maximum, or an explicit numeric value between 4 and 256.

text: Task placement in Polaris is affinitized to compute by consistently assigning the same data cells to the same nodes, preserving SQL Server buffer-pool and local SSD caches across topology changes: shrinking the topology loses only the caches of removed nodes, and growing it preserves all existing caches while only new nodes warm up.

text: Real-Time Intelligence in Fabric is a complete end-to-end solution covering data ingestion, transformation, storage, modeling, analytics, visualization, and automated actions — all purpose-built for event-driven and streaming scenarios.

sources.title: What Is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?

text: Real-Time hub functions as an organization-wide catalog of data in motion, surfacing active data streams, Microsoft-managed sources (including CDC feeds from Azure SQL DB, Cosmos DB, and PostgreSQL), and Fabric workspace item events — all accessible to every Fabric workload.

sources.title: What Is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?

text: Eventstreams provide a no-code pipeline for collecting, transforming, and routing high-volume real-time data to multiple destinations simultaneously. Supported sources include Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT v3.1/v3.1.1, and an MQTT-based Real-Time Weather connector.

sources.title: What Is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?

text: Eventstreams expose built-in stream processing operators — filtering, cleansing, windowed aggregations, deduplication, and content-based routing — so data can be shaped before landing at a destination. Derived eventstreams can also be produced as reusable, shareable outputs of these transformations.

sources.title: What Is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?

text: Activator monitors data flowing through Real-Time hub, KQL queries, or Power BI reports and fires automated actions — such as sending notifications, launching Fabric pipeline or Spark job or Dataflow executions, calling User Data Functions, or triggering Power Automate workflows — when threshold, pattern, or KQL-defined conditions are met.

sources.title: What Is Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric?

text: Fabric events and Azure Blob Storage events exposed in Real-Time hub can trigger Activator rules to start Spark jobs or Dataflows, enabling fully event-driven orchestration that requires no polling schedule.

text: As of the current NEE release, structured streaming, ANSI SQL mode, and JSON/XML source formats are not accelerated and always execute on JVM Spark; Python and Scala UDFs and complex types (arrays, maps, structs) are now supported natively, and CSV is now handled through a vectorized native parser rather than falling back.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: NEE preserves Fabric Spark's existing query optimizer behaviors — adaptive query execution, cost-based rewrites, column pruning, and predicate pushdown — so these still apply even to queries where some operators are offloaded to the native path and others fall back to the JVM.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: NEE supports parallel Delta snapshot loading and accelerates read operations on Delta tables organized with Z-ordering or Liquid Clustering, giving additional gains on top of raw operator vectorization when the underlying data layout is optimized.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: NEE casting from DECIMAL to FLOAT diverges from vanilla Spark: Spark preserves precision by round-tripping the value through a string conversion, while Velox casts directly from the internal int128_t representation, which can produce different rounding results for the same input.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: collect_list() and collect_set() use ARRAY as their intermediate aggregation type under NEE, whereas vanilla Spark uses BINARY; this type mismatch can cause query-planning or execution compatibility issues in mixed or migrated workloads that assume Spark's default intermediate representation.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: When spark.sql.mapKeyDedupPolicy is set to EXCEPTION, vanilla Spark throws an error on duplicate keys passed to map(), but NEE currently skips this duplicate-key check entirely and silently returns a result keyed on the last-seen value instead of failing.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: Whether an operator actually executed on the native path can be confirmed via Spark UI or df.explain() output — native operators carry suffixes like *Transformer, *NativeFileScan, or *VeloxColumnarToRowExec — or via the dedicated 'Gluten SQL / DataFrame' tab and its query execution graph, where green nodes denote native execution and light blue nodes denote JVM fallback.

sources.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering

text: Independent GA benchmark results reported by the Fabric product team showed roughly 4x faster query execution on a 1 TB TPC-DS workload versus vanilla Spark, and up to 6x end-to-end improvement on representative big-data jobs and typical aggregation/join queries, with NEE included at no additional cost over standard Spark capacity billing.

text: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric is built on the Hyperscale distributed-functions architecture: Microsoft Learn's Hyperscale architecture reference is versioned to explicitly cover SQL database in Fabric alongside Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on Azure VMs, confirming this is the same underlying engine design rather than a separate implementation.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: Hyperscale departs from traditional monolithic database engines by architecturally separating the relational query-processing engine from long-term data storage and durability, which is what allows storage capacity to scale out smoothly up to 128 TB for a single database.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: The engine is composed of four cooperating component types — compute nodes, page servers, a log service, and Azure Storage — all communicating over Azure's redundant network infrastructure, rather than a single process handling query, log, and storage duties together.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: Compute nodes run the same relational/language/query/transaction-processing engine used across other Azure SQL Database tiers, and each maintains a local SSD-based cache called RBPEX (Resilient Buffer Pool Extension) that is sized to the compute tier and minimizes round-trips to remote page servers for hot data pages.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: The compute topology consists of exactly one primary node handling read-write transactions, up to four on-demand high-availability secondary replicas that act as hot standbys and can offload read workloads, up to 30 named replicas for OLTP read-scale-out and HTAP scenarios (each of which can itself have up to 4 HA replicas), and an optional geo-secondary in another Azure region for disaster recovery.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: Reading from the data lake is the dominant I/O cost for warehouse queries, so the engine layers local caches (memory and SSD) over remote storage to cut the number of remote reads.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: On first access the engine transcodes data from its file-based format into a compressed columnar in-memory representation; storing each column's values together improves compression and lets operations on one column avoid touching the others.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: The columnar in-memory cache layout enables parallel execution across columns, so the engine can exploit multi-core processors when scanning, filtering, and aggregating large datasets.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Anything loaded into the in-memory cache is also serialized to a local SSD disk cache, which acts as a larger second tier for datasets that exceed memory capacity.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Because the SSD cache is larger than the in-memory cache, data evicted from memory typically survives on SSD; rehydrating memory from the SSD cache is much faster than refetching from remote storage, smoothing out query performance.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Cache eviction is recency-based: when the cache hits its capacity threshold while new data is read in, the objects unused for the longest time are removed first.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: The cache maintains full transactional consistency: DML changes to data in storage after it was cached still yield consistent query results.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Users cannot disable, configure, or manually clear the warehouse caches; Microsoft Fabric orchestrates cache management entirely, and Microsoft notes disabling it would visibly degrade query performance.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: In-memory and disk caching are distinct from result set caching, which is a separate warehouse feature: the former cache the data being scanned, the latter caches completed query results.

sources.title: In-memory and disk caching in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: The warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint automatically create and maintain histogram statistics, average column length statistics, and table cardinality statistics, which the query optimizer uses to cost and choose plans; CREATE/UPDATE STATISTICS remain available for single-column histograms during maintenance windows.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: A query's first execution can suffer a cold start: data must be fetched from OneLake into cache, statistics may need to be generated on first access, and paused compute nodes must resume (node resume or creation typically takes under one second). Cold starts can be partial, with some nodes or data already warm.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Detect cold starts via the queryinsights.exec_requests_history view: a non-zero data_scanned_remote_storage_mb means data came from OneLake during execution, while zero means the query was served entirely from cache. Never judge performance from a first run.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Oversized string types hurt performance: declare varchar(n) sized to the real data instead of varchar(8000) or varchar(max), because statistics and cost estimation get less accurate as declared length diverges from actual values. Spark string columns created without a length are seen by the warehouse as varchar(8000).

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Because warehouse data lives in immutable Parquet files, transaction rollback is fast: the engine simply reverts to the previous file versions rather than undoing row changes.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE appends a JSON file to the table's Delta transaction log; automatic checkpointing periodically summarizes the log into a checkpoint file so readers only parse the latest checkpoint plus newer entries instead of the whole log history, sharply cutting metadata I/O on frequently updated tables.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: For organisations with data already in Azure SQL Database, Fabric Mirroring provides a low-latency, low-cost path to continuously replicate that existing estate into Fabric's OneLake without rebuilding the source database.

sources.title: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric — Overview

text: Database portability is handled via SqlPackage, which supports .bacpac import/export and .dacpac schema deployments, enabling migration between Azure SQL Database and Fabric SQL database and supporting CI/CD-style incremental schema changes through SQL projects.

sources.title: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric — Overview

text: Warehouse tables are physically stored as Delta tables (Parquet data files plus a file-based transaction log), the same open format used for all Fabric data, so engineers and business users can share data without separate copies.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Warehouse data is automatically published to OneLake Files in Delta format, making the same tables readable by external engines and other Fabric workloads without export jobs.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Development is primarily in T-SQL on a large SQL Database Engine surface area, including full multi-table ACID transactions, materialized views, functions, and stored procedures.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Storage and compute are separated in the warehouse, which allows near-instant scaling, and workload management is autonomous: the distributed query engine has no user-facing tuning knobs.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: A warehouse can be loaded through several routes: the COPY INTO T-SQL command, Data Factory pipelines, Dataflows, Spark bulk writes directly to the Delta tables, or cross-database CTAS / INSERT..SELECT / SELECT INTO statements.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Cross-database queries let a single T-SQL statement combine multiple Fabric data sources in the workspace with zero data duplication.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Warehouses, Fabric SQL databases, and OneLake all automatically provision a SQL analytics endpoint at creation, built on the same engine technology as the warehouse itself.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Choose a warehouse over a lakehouse when you want enterprise-scale T-SQL-first work over structured or semi-structured data with minimal setup; choose a lakehouse when Spark is the primary tool over heterogeneous, largely unstructured data. Both run the same SQL engine for T-SQL queries, and either can be added later.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: Every Lakehouse gets an autogenerated SQL analytics endpoint that exposes its Delta tables to T-SQL for read-only querying: you can create views, inline table-valued functions, and procedures and manage object permissions, but you cannot modify the underlying data through it.

sources.title: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?

text: High-availability and named replicas share the same underlying storage components as the primary, so spinning up a new replica requires no data-copy step; only a geo-secondary replica maintains separate storage components, since it exists specifically for regional data protection and redundancy.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: The log service is the propagation backbone of Hyperscale: it accepts transaction log records from the primary compute node and fans them out both to page servers, which apply the changes to their owned pages, and to secondary compute replicas, which replay only the changes already resident in their buffer pool or RBPEX cache — then persists the log records to Azure Storage, which is treated as virtually infinite and removes the need for frequent log truncation.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: Because log growth causes such as missed log backups or slow replication to secondaries are architecturally eliminated by the log service's continuous fan-out and durable persistence to Azure Storage, Hyperscale databases avoid a common source of storage pressure seen in traditional engines.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: Backups are implemented as storage snapshots of data files rather than traditional full/differential/log backup chains, so restore operations are fast regardless of overall database size and a database can be restored to any point in time within its backup retention period.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: The architectural separation of compute and storage means the two dimensions scale independently of each other, which is the structural reason SQL database in Fabric can grow storage or add read compute without impacting the primary OLTP engine's write path.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: This Hyperscale-derived separation of the transactional compute engine from durable storage is architecturally consistent with SQL database in Fabric's separate replication path that mirrors data changes into Delta Parquet in OneLake, since the underlying engine is already designed to propagate changes to consumers other than the primary compute node without disrupting it.

sources.title: Hyperscale distributed functions architecture - Azure SQL Database

text: A background data compaction service automatically merges small Parquet files and removes logically deleted rows; since October 2025 compaction preemption makes it check for shared locks held by user queries and wait or abort rather than commit a conflicting write, though write-write conflicts with explicit user transactions remain possible.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: Avoid trickle DML: each small INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE writes a new Parquet file, producing fragmented row groups, slower scans, higher cost, and more reliance on background compaction. Batch writes instead and perform updates and deletes in batches.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: For COPY INTO (or its synonym BULK INSERT), Microsoft recommends source files between 100 MB and 1 GB, many files to maximize parallelism, parallel COPY INTO statements into different tables, and scaling to a larger capacity for big volumes.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: V-Order, a write-time Parquet sorting and compression optimization, is enabled by default on all warehouses to speed reads; it adds a small ingestion overhead, and once disabled on a warehouse it cannot be re-enabled. A common pattern is a V-Order-disabled staging warehouse for heavy ingestion feeding a V-Order-enabled warehouse for reads.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: T-SQL data clustering (in CREATE TABLE and CTAS) orders rows along a space-filling curve so similar values across the clustering columns land in adjacent storage; clustering metadata embedded in the manifest at ingestion lets the engine skip entire files and row groups outside a filter predicate's range, and the benefit grows with table size.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: The warehouse runs on a massively parallel processing (MPP) architecture, but some semantics (TOP, global sorts, final result merging) force single-node execution and trigger a 'non-scalable operation' warning; reduce the filtered dataset or apply OPTION (FORCE DISTRIBUTED PLAN) when single-node execution is not semantically required.

sources.title: Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse

text: By default, the compute available to a Fabric Warehouse is split evenly (50/50) into two isolated resource pools — a SELECT pool for all SELECT queries and a non-SELECT pool for ETL/ingestion operations; each pool scales independently but never exceeds 50% of total compute, so ingestion cannot starve read queries; workspace admins can replace this default with custom SQL pools.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: The Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint enforce a limit of 2048 user sessions per workspace, returning an explicit error when the limit is reached; DMVs show both user sessions and the many system sessions Fabric runs as a SaaS platform.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: A Fabric workspace is a natural isolation boundary of the distributed SQL compute system: a recommended pattern is to use OneLake shortcuts to expose read-only replicas of tables in other workspaces, spreading load across multiple SQL engines and effectively raising the ceiling on concurrent read-only sessions.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: Warehouse workloads benefit from burstable capacity, which lets jobs temporarily consume extra resources for better performance, and from smoothing, which spreads the evaluation of compute consumption over time so spiky peak-time usage is offset against idle periods.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: When a query arrives, the SQL frontend optimizes it and hands the plan to the Distributed Query Processing (DQP) engine, which splits it into smaller queries called tasks — the units of distributed execution — that run on backend compute nodes; results flow back through the frontend to the caller.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: A Fabric warehouse task reads files from OneLake, joins, groups, or orders data produced by other tasks, and for ingestion jobs writes results to the destination tables — so both query and ingest paths run through the same task-based distributed engine.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: The DQP scheduler operates at task level and represents each query as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks, so tasks without mutual dependencies can execute simultaneously or out of order, giving both intra-query parallelism and cross-query concurrency.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: Incoming tasks are scheduled on first-in-first-out principles, but when idle capacity exists the scheduler can switch to a best-fit placement approach to improve concurrency.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: When the scheduler detects resource pressure it autonomously triggers a scale-out of the backend topology; because acquiring new nodes typically takes a few seconds (with no SLA on assignment), the engine is not optimized for consistently sub-second latency on queries that need distributed processing.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: Scaling of the warehouse backend is an online operation — in-flight query processing continues uninterrupted while nodes are added — and when pressure subsides the topology scales back down and returns compute to the region.

sources.title: Workload Management in Fabric Data Warehouse (Microsoft Learn)

text: The engine is fault tolerant at the task level: if a backend node becomes unhealthy, the operations running on it are redistributed to healthy nodes for completion rather than failing the query.
